title: Add a test runner that can run tests in parallel and in network namespaces with temporary directories.
author: fruffy

title: Clarification on Meter Configuration Units and Granularity in TNA
body:
Hi,

I'm trying to understand how to configure direct and indirect meters on a switch, but I am stuck because I do not understand in which units and with which granularity $METER_SPEC_CIR_PPS, $METER_SPEC_PIR_PPS, $METER_SPEC_CBS_PKTS and $METER_SPEC_PBS_PKTS parameters are expressed.

I initially thought that the units were:

- **Number of packets** for the CBS and PBS parameters (and I am pretty sure about this);
- **Packets per second** for the CIR and PIR parameters (but I don't think so for the last one).

Furthermore, I noticed that the CIR and PIR seem to be multiples of 9, but I do not understand why.

These might be trivial questions, but since I’m new to the TNA architecture, I do not know how to proceed.

I would really appreciate any support or clarification.

I would also like to ask if it is possible to add documentation about the bfrt_grpc Python package in this repository or provide information on where to find it.

Thank you for your time!
author: AnToN1o99

comments.body:
@AnToN1o99 -- the parameters you mention are specified in packets-per-second (CIR and PIR) and packets (CBS and PBS), exactly as their names state. Internally they are represented as custom floating point numbers and thus the API implementation rounds the number to the nearest representable value, so what you read back is not necessarily exactly what you put in. 

Here is an example:
```python
def print_meter(idx):
    m = bfrt.simple_l3_meter.pipe.Ingress.packet_meter.get(idx, print_ents=False)
    print(f"Meter {m.key[b'$METER_INDEX']}: CIR: {m.data[b'$METER_SPEC_CIR_PPS']}pps CBS: {m.data[b'$METER_
 SPEC_CBS_PKTS']}pkts PIR: {m.data[b'$METER_SPEC_PIR_PPS']}pps PBS: {m.data[b'$METER_SPEC_PBS_PKTS']}pkts")

for i in range(7):
    mod(METER_INDEX=i,
            METER_SPEC_CIR_PPS=10**(i+1),
            METER_SPEC_CBS_PKTS=10**(i+2), 
            METER_SPEC_PIR_PPS=10**(i+3),
            METER_SPEC_PBS_PKTS=10**(i+4))
  print_meter(i)
```

Output:
```
Meter 0: CIR: 9 pps   CBS: 100 pkts   PIR: 994 pps   PBS: 9984 pkts
Meter 1: CIR: 94 pps   CBS: 1000 pkts   PIR: 9999 pps   PBS: 99840 pkts
Meter 2: CIR: 994 pps   CBS: 9984 pkts   PIR: 99999 pps   PBS: 999424 pkts
Meter 3: CIR: 9999 pps   CBS: 99840 pkts   PIR: 998787 pps   PBS: 9961472 pkts
Meter 4: CIR: 99999 pps   CBS: 999424 pkts   PIR: 9968476 pps   PBS: 99614720 pkts
Meter 5: CIR: 998787 pps   CBS: 9961472 pkts   PIR: 99917488 pps   PBS: 998244352 pkts
Meter 6: CIR: 9968476 pps   CBS: 99614720 pkts   PIR: 997933632 pps   PBS: 9999220736 pkts
```

As for the documentation, I suggest you create a separate issue.

To answer your last question (why the values programmed in the hardware look a certain way), please understand that what is programmed inside the hardware is not really the rate in pps or the burst size in packets. Instead, the API programs some token bucket parameters, that are ultimately tied to the device clock frequency, which is normally equal to 1.22 GHz (if we talk about Tofino1).

@AnToN1o99 -- if something doesn't work as expected at runtime, the proper procedure to get help is as follows:

1. Provide the full source code of the program
2. Provide the PTF test that demonstrates the problem (i.e. it should succeed, but fails instead)

In your case, it is also important to mention whether you are trying to do this on a real device or on the model

While running new tests I found a solution to my problem, and now my network is working as expected. 
Thank you again for your support.
@pkotikal You need to fix up DCO on your commit.

title: hw/rdc_setup.sh: fix typos, add missing files
body:
This PR contains the changes that I found necessary for building the project for the Tofino reference platforms.

Apart from some obvious typos and missing directories for source and header files, it appears to me that the `libavago` pre-built binaries need to be copied as well.
author: alexandergall

comments.body: @vgurevich @pkotikal Would one of you be able to try this out?  I do not think Fabian has access to the proprietary Intel software to try this out, and I do not.

@jafingerhut -- I do not have access to Tofino HW at the moment. But I'd trust @alexandergall :) I was also surprised seeing the `avago` directory missing in the original code, so this makes sense to me for sure.

> @jafingerhut -- I do not have access to Tofino HW at the moment. But I'd trust @alexandergall :) I was also surprised seeing the `avago` directory missing in the original code, so this makes sense to me for sure.

I was mainly thinking of trying out the script with the mix of open-p4studio and proprietary Intel software to see if the script runs without error.  Testing it on hardware afterwards is of course ideal, but verifying that the script actually runs for one more person other than the one who wrote it is a far better check than only the one person who wrote it.

If that isn't possible, no worries.  Just hoping for at least a _little bit_ of testing or review on this.
@ansamalintel, can you please look into this?

@jafingerhut -- I decided to give it a try, but one thing I can see right away is that the instructions in the `README.md` are kinda incomplete and the script will require further enhancements for usability. Let me try to build the way I think it **should** work and we'll see what will happen.

```bash
OS_BFD="/home/ubuntu/op4-rdc/open-p4studio/pkgsrc/bf-drivers"
```


If it is a 4vCPU 16GB RAM instance with no swap, it could end up significantly slower, or failing.  At least that is what Vlad saw on an AWS instance he tried this on a while ago.

> > Yeah, I just noted that because I saw current CI uses 3 jobs instead of 4.
> 
> If it is a 4vCPU 16GB RAM instance with no swap, it could end up significantly slower, or failing. At least that is what Vlad saw on an AWS instance he tried this on a while ago.

The Tofino back end unified build uses somewhere around 5-6 GB of RAM on a very few individual processes, is why.  Vlad suggested the idea of disabling unified build option -- more processes to run, but no individual huge-memory ones that cause you to want to reduce the number of parallel jobs.

> The Tofino back end unified build uses somewhere around 5-6 GB of RAM on a very few individual processes, is why. Vlad suggested the idea of disabling unified build option -- more processes to run, but no individual huge-memory ones that cause you to want to reduce the number of parallel jobs.

In my experience a unified build outperforms even multiple cores but we can tweak the "chunk size" of the build to reduce the memory usage.

My suggestion is to have a swap file and then implement #72. Essentially, all we need to take the min of 15% RAM and 25% Swap and add that amount to the total size of RAM before calculating the amount of RAM per CPU. Having 15% of RAM in the swap does not usually impact the performance. 

It also makes sense to have swap anyway, just for the sake of safety.

I think this PR is ready to merge, if you approve.

All of the suggestions for detecting swap space and using that to determine the number of parallel jobs to run has a separate issue created to track it already.  I am not planning to implement that in this PR.

It also adds to the behavior of the `p4studio profile apply <profile_name>` command the calculation of a number of jobs that should avoid memory use from exceeding the memory available on the system (as long as you don't run any heavy-memory-use processes while doing the build -- we can't guard against that except by advice to people).

FYI, you can still specify the number of parallel jobs if you want to using the `--jobs <n>` command line option to p4studio.  The new behavior of calculating a reasonable number is only present if you omit that option.

title: Use the system-level Python for bf-python instead of a hardcoded 3.10 cpython.
body:
Or install the system version of cpython instead of a fixed 3.10. 
E.g., 3.8 for Ubuntu 20.04, 3.10 for Ubuntu 22.04, 3.12 for Ubuntu.24.04
author: fruffy

comments.body:
I do not have ready examples to give, but I believe that Python 3.y > Python 3.x sometimes introduces backwards incompatibilities, despite not bumping the major version number (i.e. either they do not use semantic versioning, or they only pay it lip service and don't really follow it).  That combined with Python's dynamic nature means that extensive testing of a large fraction of code paths might be required to ensure that a different version of Python will be suitable for using here.

I have no problem trying it out, mind you.  Just that by using different versions of Python on different OS's, we could be introducing failures that will be time-consuming to find later.

This PEP says that developers are explicitly allowed to introduce backwards incompatible changes if there are warnings for at least 2 minor releases before the change is made, e.g. warnings in python3.8 and python3.9, then backwards incompatible change in python3.10.

I do _not_ know if those warnings must occur at Python compile time.  Given its dynamic nature, I would bet $100 that some of them only occur when the relevant method or function is actually called at run time, and then only if the warnings are enabled, and then you might not even see them unless you look for them in the right place, e.g. buried in some log file, or redirected to /dev/null.

There are actual reasons people pin versions of Python.

It is much easier to maintain a system for a single Python version than for an interleaving of different Python versions. It is also harder to debug system-level Python incompatibilities, e.g, a particular Python versions incompatibility with the OS-level `glibc` etc. 

The backwards incompatible changes between Python versions are usually manageable and can be addressed in the Python code, the system-level incompatibilities less so. 

Ubuntu is also fairly good at sticking with a particular version of Python, which means we can make better guarantees and test for that particular version. If users use a different version than what is tested on CI that is on them. 


The best solution is to use a venv. Poetry, or uv, but that requires more invasive changes.
Is this one closable as fixed by p4lang/open-p4studio-old#25 too?
No, the problem is not resolved. We actually just disabled bf-python to work around the mismatch. It doesn't look like it is needed yet.
